questions.question: Define monopoly, list the main barriers to entry, and explain — with a numerical illustration — why the monopolist's marginal revenue curve lies below its demand curve.
questions.expected_answer: A monopoly is a market with one seller of a product that has no close substitutes, protected by blocked entry. Barriers include legal protection (patents, licences, exclusive franchises), control of an essential resource, natural monopoly (one network is cheaper than two — a single transmission grid or water pipe), and economies of scale no entrant can match. Because the monopolist is the industry, it faces the downward-sloping market demand curve and is a price maker. To sell an extra unit it must lower the price on every unit, not just the last one: selling 20 units at R50 or 21 at R49 means the 21st unit brings in R49 but costs R1 off each of the other 20, so its marginal revenue is R49 − R20 = R29, well below the price. Hence MR starts at the same intercept as demand and falls twice as steeply, lying below D = AR. Output is chosen where MR = MC, price is read off the demand curve above that quantity, and — because entry is blocked — economic profit can persist into the long run, with price above marginal cost and output below the competitive level.

questions.question: Use the kinked demand curve to explain why oligopoly prices are sticky, and describe both forms of collusion together with the reasons cartels tend to break down.
questions.expected_answer: Oligopolists are mutually interdependent, so each firm anticipates rivals' reactions. The firm's demand curve kinks at the ruling price: above the kink it is elastic, because a firm raising its price alone is not followed and loses customers heavily; below the kink it is inelastic, because a price cut is matched, so volumes barely change while revenue falls. Raising loses alone and cutting gains nothing, so prices stay sticky — the kink even breaks the MR curve with a vertical gap, meaning modest cost changes leave price unchanged. Competition therefore shifts to non-price weapons: branding, advertising, loyalty programmes, features, service and sponsorship. Collusion is the escape from rivalry: overt collusion (a cartel) has the few agree on prices or divide markets, jointly earning monopoly profit — South African bread and construction cases are examples prosecuted under the Competition Act; tacit collusion is quieter, as in price leadership where the dominant firm moves and the rest follow. Cartels are unstable because each member profits from secretly undercutting the agreement, and they are illegal, exposing members to Commission investigation and Tribunal fines of up to ten percent of annual turnover.

questions.question: Explain the long-run equilibrium of a monopolistically competitive firm and evaluate the efficiency of the four market structures side by side.
questions.expected_answer: In monopolistic competition, differentiation gives each of many sellers a gently downward-sloping demand curve, so short-run economic profit is possible using the monopoly-style diagram (MR = MC, price off the demand curve). But entry is free: profit attracts newcomers who shave away customers, shifting each incumbent's demand curve left until it is tangent to the AC curve at the chosen output — price equals average cost, normal profit only. Because the demand curve slopes, the tangency lies left of AC's minimum, so the firm carries excess capacity (produces below its cheapest scale), and price still exceeds marginal cost, so allocative efficiency also fails mildly; the compensation is variety. Comparison: perfect competition alone achieves both allocative (P = MC) and productive (minimum AC) efficiency; monopolistic competition misses both narrowly, paying for choice with excess capacity; oligopoly restricts output, keeps prices sticky and diverts resources into persuasion, though scale and innovation partly compensate; monopoly restricts output most and prices furthest above marginal cost, with persistent profit behind blocked entry — qualified by the natural monopoly case, where one producer genuinely is cheapest and regulation beats break-up, and by the possibility that large profits fund major research. All four are generated by two settings: the slope of the firm's demand curve and the ease of entry.
